introduction-the-journey-of-a-write.core: A write() travels a long path. The syscall enters the VFS, the filesystem (ext4, XFS) maps it to blocks, and data lands in the page cache (dirty pages); the call returns. Later, writeback creates bios for the block layer, I/O schedulers and multi-queue (blk-mq) dispatch them to the driver (NVMe or SCSI), and the device's own cache and firmware finally persist them. Durability needs fsync to force every layer to flush.

first_principles.problem: An app writes data, gets success, the server loses power, and the data is gone.

analogy.title: Posting a letter
analogy.story: Dropping it in a postbox (write) feels done, but it goes through collection, sorting and delivery; only a signed receipt (fsync) proves it arrived.
analogy.breaks: Letters rarely vanish; unflushed page cache is lost on power failure.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Data survives power loss after fsync returns.

code.text:
import os
fd = os.open("orders.log", os.O_WRONLY | os.O_APPEND | os.O_CREAT, 0o640)
os.write(fd, b'order 42 paid\n')    # in page cache only
os.fsync(fd)                          # forces FS + device flush
os.close(fd)

check.q: Why can data written with write() be lost after it returns success?
check.a: It's often only in the page cache (and device caches); without fsync it hasn't been persisted to stable storage.

the-virtual-filesystem-vfs-one-api-to-ru.core: The VFS is the kernel's abstraction layer that gives every filesystem (ext4, XFS, Btrfs, NFS, tmpfs, procfs, FUSE) the same API: open, read, write, stat, mmap. It maintains common objects (superblocks, inodes, dentries and the dentry cache, open files) and dispatches operations to each filesystem's implementation through operation tables. That's why cat works identically on a local disk, NFS or /proc, and why dentry and inode caches speed up path lookups.

first_principles.problem: Engineers wonder why listing a huge directory is fast the second time and slow after a reboot.
derivation: Mount table joins **filesystems into one tree**.

analogy.title: A universal remote control
analogy.story: One set of buttons works across TVs from different makers, each translating the commands internally.
analogy.breaks: Remotes don't cache; VFS caches names and metadata aggressively.

code.text:
time ls -R /usr >/dev/null      # cold: 2.1 s
time ls -R /usr >/dev/null      # warm: 0.3 s (dcache/icache)
vfsstat-bpfcc 1 3                # VFS ops per second

check.q: What does the dentry cache speed up?
check.a: Path name lookups, by caching directory entries mapping names to inodes.

buffered-io-vs-direct-io.core: Buffered I/O goes through the page cache: reads may be served from memory, readahead prefetches sequential data, and writes are absorbed and flushed later. That's great for most workloads. Direct I/O (O_DIRECT) bypasses the page cache, moving data between user buffers and the device, which needs aligned buffers and offsets. Databases with their own buffer pools use it to avoid double caching and to control I/O timing.

first_principles.problem: A database caches data in its buffer pool and the OS page cache, wasting half the RAM.
truths: The page cache helps generic workloads.
Apps with their own caches double-cache.

analogy.title: Using a shared warehouse vs your own stockroom
analogy.story: Most shops use the shared warehouse; a big store with its own stockroom ships straight to it, avoiding storing goods twice.
analogy.breaks: Stockrooms don't need alignment; O_DIRECT requires block-aligned I/O.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No double caching for the DB.

check.q: Why do some databases use O_DIRECT?
check.a: They manage their own buffer cache, so bypassing the page cache avoids double caching and gives them control over I/O.

synchronous-vs-asynchronous-io.core: Synchronous blocking I/O (read or write) makes the thread wait until data is ready or accepted, which is simple but needs one thread per concurrent operation. Non-blocking I/O returns EAGAIN if not ready, so readiness notification (select, poll, epoll) lets one thread manage many sockets. True asynchronous I/O submits operations and is notified on completion (Linux AIO for direct I/O, io_uring for everything). Event-driven servers combine non-blocking sockets with readiness or completion APIs to scale.

first_principles.problem: A server using a thread per connection collapses at 10,000 concurrent clients.
truths: The kernel can notify readiness or completion.

analogy.title: Waiting at each shop counter vs leaving orders and getting texts
analogy.story: Blocking is standing in line; async is leaving the order and being texted when it's ready.
analogy.breaks: Texts arrive by phone; I/O completions arrive via kernel queues.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Scales to 10k+ connections on one core.

code.text:
import asyncio
async def handle(reader, writer):
    data = await reader.read(4096)     # yields instead of blocking a thread
    writer.write(data); await writer.drain(); writer.close()
async def main():
    server = await asyncio.start_server(handle, '0.0.0.0', 8080)
    async with server: await server.serve_forever()
asyncio.run(main())   # thousands of connections, one thread

check.q: What's the difference between readiness-based and completion-based async I/O?
check.a: Readiness APIs (epoll) say when an operation can proceed without blocking; completion APIs (io_uring) tell you when a submitted operation has finished.

generation-1-select-and-poll.core: select() and poll() let one thread wait on many file descriptors. You pass the full set of FDs of interest, the kernel scans every one, sleeps until one is ready, and returns, and then you scan the set again to find which. Cost is O(n) per call in both kernel and user space, select is limited to 1,024 FDs (FD_SETSIZE), and the whole set is copied each time. That's fine for dozens of connections and painful for tens of thousands.

first_principles.problem: A chat server using select() stalls when connections exceed 1,024 and burns CPU at 5,000.
truths: Passing all FDs each call is O(n).
Scanning many idle FDs wastes time.

analogy.title: Asking every guest at a party whether they need a drink, every minute
analogy.story: Fine for ten guests; with ten thousand you spend all your time asking.
analogy.breaks: Party hosts remember who asked; select/poll keep no state between calls.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Works, but cost grows with total connections.

check.q: Why do select and poll scale poorly to many connections?
check.a: Every call passes and scans the entire FD set, so cost is O(n) even when few descriptors are ready.

generation-2-epoll-the-event-list.core: epoll keeps the interest set in the kernel. epoll_create makes an instance, epoll_ctl adds, modifies or removes FDs once, and epoll_wait returns only the ready FDs. Cost scales with ready events, not total FDs, which solved C10K for nginx, Node.js (libuv), Redis and Netty. Edge-triggered mode reports state changes and needs draining until EAGAIN; level-triggered reports while ready. EPOLLEXCLUSIVE helps avoid thundering herds.

first_principles.problem: A proxy must handle 100,000 mostly idle WebSocket connections on a few cores.

analogy.title: Guests raising their hand when they need something
analogy.story: The host registers everyone once, then only attends to raised hands.
analogy.breaks: Hands stay up until served; edge-triggered epoll notifies once per change.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 100k idle connections cost nothing per wait.

check.q: Why doesn't epoll help with regular file I/O?
check.a: Regular files are always reported 'ready'; reads can still block on disk, so completion-based APIs like io_uring are needed.

generation-3-io_uring-the-new-king.core: io_uring (Linux 5.1+) uses two ring buffers shared between user space and the kernel: a submission queue and a completion queue. Apps write requests (read, write, accept, send, fsync, openat and many more) into the SQ and reap results from the CQ, batching many operations per syscall, or none with SQPOLL kernel polling. It provides true async for files and sockets, fixed buffers and files, and linked ops. It's very fast, but it has had security issues and some environments disable it.

first_principles.problem: A storage service doing millions of small random reads spends most CPU on syscall overhead.

analogy.title: A conveyor belt between restaurant and kitchen
analogy.story: Waiters place many orders on the belt and collect finished dishes from another belt, without walking into the kitchen for each.
analogy.breaks: Belts are physical; rings are shared memory requiring careful ordering.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Syscall overhead cut by an order of magnitude.

check.q: How does io_uring reduce syscall overhead?
check.a: Requests and completions are exchanged through shared-memory rings, allowing many operations per submit syscall (or none with SQPOLL).

the-block-layer-and-the-bio-struct.core: Below filesystems, the block layer handles requests to block devices. Filesystems build bios (block I/O descriptors listing device, sector and memory segments), which are merged into requests, scheduled, and dispatched through blk-mq: per-CPU software queues mapped to hardware queues, which matters for NVMe with up to 64K queues. Stats in /sys/block/<dev>/stat and iostat (r/s, w/s, await, aqu-sz, %util) and tracing (blktrace, biolatency) observe it.

first_principles.problem: An NVMe drive rated at 1M IOPS delivers only 200k because the application issues I/O with queue depth 1.
truths: Block requests carry sectors and buffers.

analogy.title: Mail being bundled and routed to many loading bays
analogy.story: Letters (bios) going to the same street are bundled (merged), then sent to many bays (hardware queues) at once.
analogy.breaks: Mail bays are few; NVMe has thousands of queues.

code.text:
fio --name=qd1  --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=1  --ioengine=io_uring --direct=1 --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --runtime=20 --time_based --readonly
fio --name=qd64 --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=64 --ioengine=io_uring --direct=1 --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --runtime=20 --time_based --readonly
iostat -x 1 nvme0n1     # aqu-sz shows queue depth in use

check.q: Why is %util in iostat misleading for NVMe devices?
check.a: NVMe processes many requests in parallel, so 100% util (time busy) doesn't mean the device is saturated.

io-schedulers-the-elevator-algorithm.core: I/O schedulers order and merge requests. Classic elevators reordered by sector to minimise disk head seeks on HDDs. Modern blk-mq schedulers: none (pass-through, often best for fast NVMe), mq-deadline (bounded latency with read priority; good for SATA SSDs and HDDs), bfq (fairness per process, desktop interactivity, and cgroup io.weight proportional sharing) and kyber (latency targets for fast devices). Choose per device via /sys/block/<dev>/queue/scheduler.

first_principles.problem: An HDD-based backup server has erratic latency with 'none', while an NVMe database is slowed by bfq overhead.
truths: Fast devices suffer from scheduler overhead.

analogy.title: A lift deciding stop order
analogy.story: For a slow old lift, sweeping floors in order saves time; for an instant teleporter, just go where asked.
analogy.breaks: Lifts carry people; schedulers also enforce fairness and deadlines.

code.text:
# /etc/udev/rules.d/60-iosched.rules
ACTION=="add|change", KERNEL=="nvme[0-9]*n[0-9]*", ATTR{queue/scheduler}="none"
ACTION=="add|change", KERNEL=="sd[a-z]", ATTR{queue/rotational}=="1", ATTR{queue/scheduler}="mq-deadline"
# check: cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/scheduler  → [none] mq-deadline kyber bfq

check.q: Why is the 'none' scheduler often best for NVMe?
check.a: NVMe devices handle huge parallel queues with minimal latency, so extra scheduler reordering only adds CPU overhead.
